newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary supports NATO membership for Slovakia.
newsitem.headline: Hungary supports NATO membership for Slovakia.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn appealed to Poland and the Czech Republic, the other two countries now certain to be invited to join NATO, not to ignore unfavoured Slovakia in the race for European integration.

"I would like to express (Hungary's) interest in Slovakia meeting the various criteria of accession into the various European organisations," Horn told reporters after a meeting with visiting Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.

Slovakia was once considered an equal candidate with its three neighbours for early NATO membership but in recent years has fallen out of consideration after Western criticism of the slow rate of reform under Prime Minister Wladimir Meciar.

The United States has named Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as its chosen three for the first wave of new NATO members to be named at the the alliance's Madrid summit next week. But southern European NATO states, notably France, are looking for Romania and Slovenia to be also included.

Horn, in another sign of Hungary's emerging role as a link with neighbouring countries unsuccessful in their efforts at early NATO membership, appealed for the "reactivation" of the political grouping, the Visegrad Four.

The grouping of Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia was formed in the early nineties and gives Slovakia equal status with its three central European allies but has been superceded in recent years by its economic equivalent, the Central European Free Trade (CEFTA).

"(Hungary's) position has always been clear that it is in our interests to have Slovakia within the process of accession," Horn said. "I am convinced that the reactivation of the Visegrad Four...would be conducive to that."

Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said on Tuesday he would prefer NATO to name not just a first group of new members next week but also all the countries that would make up the second wave of enlargement.
Cimoszewicz, on a one-day visit to Budapest, appealed for NATO not to close the door on further enlargement after Madrid but stopped short of endorsing Kovacs's position.
"I have no idea about that, it is (NATO) not us that will take that decision," he said.

Cimoszewicz confirmed that the Prime Ministers of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic would meet in the southern Polish city of Krakow on August 22 to discuss joint steps on both NATO and European Union integration ahead of expected accession talks.

"The meeting will be held after the decisions of the Madrid summit are already known and...before the commencement of accession negotiations so we can discuss what we need to do during the (Krakow) talks," he said.
